newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bonn backs DT pricing, rivals appeal to EU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn backs DT pricing, rivals appeal to EU.

text.p: In one of the first instances of mediation between Deutsche Telekom and its competitors, the German government has ruled in favour of the state-owned phone giant, saying on Friday that its pricing is not discriminatory.

But six German and U.S. companies that compete against Telekom in the corporate network services market said they would challenge the Bonn ruling and ask the European Commission to stop a new set of DT prices from taking effect next month.

The incident is an indication of just how unclear Germany's regulatory environment remains as Deutsche Telekom presents itself to international investors ahead of its huge initial public offering next month.
Telekom said its rivals complaint were unjustified.
"This is just interference by our competitors shortly before our share listing," said DT spokesman Hans Ehnert.

The ruling was issued last week but has just now become public. It is not legally binding and is the result of the government's efforts to mediate in a dispute between DT and its competitors over the prices it charges them for leasing lines to set up corporate telecommunications networks.
At issue are DT's so-called "Dial and Benefit" tariffs that are set to take effect on November 1. They offer a range of discounts to big customers based on call volume.
The top rate is a discount of 35 percent, but rivals say that under certain circumstances discounts could go as high as 49 percent and thereby end up lower than DT's leased-line charges.

"The ruling states that the Dial and Benefit tariffs are appropriate for also lowering the costs of operators of corporate networks. That means for Telekom's competitors," said post ministry spokesman Christian Hoppe.
"Deutsche Telekom's tariffs fulfil the conditions set out by the German government and the European Commission in June," he added.

The complaint was filed by Communications Network International, the Mannesmann unit, Thyssen subsidiary Plus Net, Veba's Meganet, RWE Telliance AG, WorldCom Inc and Viag Interkom, the joint venture of Viag AG and British Telecom.
Peter Bross, managing director of Mannesmann Eurokom GmbH, the engineering group's telecommunications subsidiary, said the new tariffs represented an abuse of DT's market power.
"The strategies of the newcomers for entering the market in 1998 are in danger of being destroyed. And this would endanger millions in planned investments," he told reporters in Duesseldorf.

Brussels approved the discounts in June after a lengthy dispute with German Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch and only after winning assurance from Bonn that strict conditions would be met.

The German government had to agree that "at least two licences for the construction or ownership and control of alternative infrastructure" offering telecoms services would have come into force by November.
Bonn has still not awarded any licences, but it said it had received 30 applications.

"We still need to pass a legal ordinance that regulates the charges for such licences," said Christian Hoppe, spokesman at the postal ministry. "We are confident that this issue will be cleared up and it is still possible to meet the deadline."
A spokesman for European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said the Commission had not yet received any complaint against Deutsche Telekom.
